claim: Seawater samples were collected twice a month from 11 coastal sites for 2 years between August 2017 and August 2019 at the Boso Peninsula, Japan, totaling 550 samples.
source: We collected seawater samples twice a month (i.e., around the first and second quarter moons) for 2 years between August 2017 and August 2019 at the 11 sites.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sampling frequency, duration, number of sites, and total sample count in the Methods section.

claim: The study region is located on the Pacific side of Honshu Island around 35°N and is markedly affected by the warm Kuroshio Current, cold Oyashio Current, and inner-bay water from Tokyo Bay.
source: This region is located on the Pacific side of Honshu Island around 35°N and is markedly affected by the warm Kuroshio Current, cold Oyashio Current, and inner-bay water from Tokyo Bay.
evidence: The manuscript describes the geographic and oceanographic characteristics of the study region.

claim: eDNA metabarcoding detected 856 MOTUs across 33 orders, 167 families, and 466 genera.
source: We inspected their family-level phylogenies to increase the accuracy of taxonomic assignments, recognizing 856 MOTUs across 33 orders, 167 families, and 466 genera (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The manuscript reports the taxonomic diversity detected through eDNA metabarcoding analysis.

claim: The taxonomic diversity detected was similar to that of the local fauna compiled from literature survey and museum collections (948 species across 33 orders, 158 families, and 493 genera).
source: This taxonomic diversity was similar to that of the local fauna (948 species across 33 orders, 158 families, and 493 genera) compiled from a literature survey and museum collections (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: The manuscript compares the eDNA-detected diversity with known local fauna diversity from literature and museum records.

claim: Fish eDNA concentrations and fish species richness showed a clear intra-annual pattern (seasonality), being higher in warmer months than in colder months at all sites.
source: Fish eDNA concentrations and fish species richness showed a clear intra-annual pattern (i.e., seasonality; Figure 1b, c), which were higher in warmer months (e.g., between July and October) than in colder months (e.g., between January and March) at all sites.
evidence: The manuscript describes seasonal patterns in eDNA concentrations and species richness, with reference to Figure 1b and 1c showing these patterns.

claim: Total eDNA concentrations and species richness positively correlated with water temperature.
source: Total eDNA concentrations and species richness positively correlated with water temperature (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript states a positive correlation between temperature and both eDNA concentrations and species richness, referencing a supplementary figure.

claim: Acanthopagrus schlegelii eDNA was detected in 504 out of 550 water samples (91.6%).
source: Metabarcoding detected the eDNA of A. schlegelii in 504 out of 550 water samples (91.6%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and, thus, we decided to use the sequence reads of A. schlegelii as the internal standard DNA of each sample.
evidence: The manuscript reports the detection frequency of A. schlegelii eDNA and its use as an internal standard.

claim: The negative controls produced negligible reads (177 ± 665 reads [mean ± standard deviation]), accounting for ca. 0.1% of the positive sample reads.
source: The negative controls produced negligible reads (177 ± 665 reads [mean ± standard deviation]), which accounted for ca. 0.1% of the positive sample reads.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data on contamination levels in negative controls.

claim: All reads from negative controls were assigned to non-target taxa, such as fish species that had never been observed in the study region and freshwater fish species.
source: Moreover, all of the reads were assigned to non-target taxa, such as fish species that had never been observed in the study region and freshwater fish species (possibly contaminated from the laboratory).
evidence: The manuscript describes the taxonomic assignment of reads from negative controls.

claim: The top 50 most frequently detected species had detection frequencies ranging between 148 and 532 with a mean of 296.
source: The detection frequencies of these 50 species ranged between 148 and 532 with a mean of 296, and their total detection frequencies reached 14,793 (62.0% of the total detection frequency).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on detection frequencies for the top 50 species.

claim: The total detection frequencies of the top 50 species reached 14,793, representing 62.0% of the total detection frequency.
source: The detection frequencies of these 50 species ranged between 148 and 532 with a mean of 296, and their total detection frequencies reached 14,793 (62.0% of the total detection frequency).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of total detections represented by the top 50 species.

claim: At the regional scale, the linear correlations among water temperature, total eDNA concentrations, interaction strengths, the number of interactions, and species richness were all statistically clear (p < 0.05) except for the linear correlation between water temperature and mean interaction strengths (p > 0.05).
source: At the regional scale, the linear correlations among water temperature, total eDNA concentrations, interaction strengths, the number of interactions, and species richness was all statistically clear (p < 0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) except for the linear correlation between water temperature and mean interaction strengths (p > 0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical results of linear correlations among multiple variables.

claim: Interaction strengths became weak as species richness increased.
source: The interaction strengths became weak as species richness increased, which is consistent with a previous study (Ratzke et al., 2020; Ushio, 2022a), suggesting that understanding the causes and effects of weak interactions is key to understanding the maintenance of species-rich communities.
evidence: The manuscript describes a relationship between interaction strength and species richness, citing previous studies.

claim: The largest information flow was detected from Pseudoblennius marmoratus to Pseudolabrus eoethinus.
source: The largest information flow was detected from Pseudoblennius marmoratus to Pseudolabrus eoethinus (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The manuscript identifies the strongest detected interaction in the network.

claim: Bidirectional information flow was detected between Pseudolabrus eoethinus and Gymnothorax kidako.
source: Bidirectional information flow was detected between P. eoethinus and Gymnothorax kidako.
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific bidirectional interaction detected in the network.

claim: The in-strengths and out-strengths of fish species interactions were statistically clearly associated with water temperature, species richness, and total eDNA concentration (GAMM, p < 0.05) except for the effects of species richness on the in-strengths.
source: The in-strengths and out-strengths of fish species interactions were statistically clearly associated with water temperature, species richness, and total eDNA concentration (GAMM, p < 0.05; Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1d) except for the effects on species richness on the in-strengths (Figure 3b).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical results from GAMM analysis of interaction strengths.

claim: In-strengths of the fish–fish interactions increased with water temperature.
source: In-strengths of the fish–fish interactions increased with water temperature (Figure 3a), supporting our first hypothesis while out-strengths of the interactions showed an opposite pattern (Figure 3d), which might suggest there is a difference in the temperature dependence between the in-strengths and out-strengths of the interactions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationship between in-strengths and temperature, referencing Figure 3a.

claim: Out-strengths of the interactions showed an opposite pattern to in-strengths, decreasing with water temperature.
source: In-strengths of the fish–fish interactions increased with water temperature (Figure 3a), supporting our first hypothesis while out-strengths of the interactions showed an opposite pattern (Figure 3d), which might suggest there is a difference in the temperature dependence between the in-strengths and out-strengths of the interactions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationship between out-strengths and temperature, referencing Figure 3d.

claim: Interaction strengths decreased with increasing species richness and total eDNA concentration.
source: Interaction strengths were also statistically clearly influenced by species richness and total eDNA concentrations (except for Figure 3b); the interaction strengths decreased with increasing species richness and total eDNA concentration.
evidence: The manuscript describes relationships between interaction strengths and both species richness and total eDNA concentration.

claim: In-strengths of Halichoeres tenuispinis, Macrocanthus strigatus, Pempheris schwenkii, Stethojulis interrupta terina, and Thalassoma cupido clearly increased at higher water temperatures.
source: The in-strengths of several fish species clearly increased at higher water temperatures: for example, Halichoeres tenuispinis, Macrocanthus strigatus, Pempheris schwenkii, Stethojulis interrupta terina, and Thalassoma cupido (Figure 4a).
evidence: The manuscript identifies specific species whose in-strengths increased with temperature, referencing Figure 4a.

claim: In-strengths of Ditrema temminckii temminckii, Engraulis japonicus, and Girella punctata decreased at higher water temperatures.
source: On the other hand, in-strengths of some fish species and out-strengths decreased at higher water temperatures: for example, in-strengths of Ditrema temminckii temminckii, Engraulis japonicus, and Girella punctata, and out-strengths of five fish species (Figure 4a, b).
evidence: The manuscript identifies specific species whose in-strengths decreased with temperature, referencing Figure 4a and 4b.

claim: Out-strengths of five fish species decreased at higher water temperatures.
source: On the other hand, in-strengths of some fish species and out-strengths decreased at higher water temperatures: for example, in-strengths of Ditrema temminckii temminckii, Engraulis japonicus, and Girella punctata, and out-strengths of five fish species (Figure 4a, b).
evidence: The manuscript states that out-strengths of five species decreased with temperature, referencing Figure 4a and 4b.

claim: The dominance of weak interactions stabilizes the dynamics of a natural fish community.
source: The dominance of weak interactions stabilizes the dynamics of a natural fish community (Ushio et al., 2018a).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study about the stabilizing effect of weak interactions.

claim: Interaction strengths have been reported to decrease with increases in the diversity of experimental microbial communities.
source: Interaction strengths have been reported to decrease with increases in the diversity of experimental microbial communities (Ratzke et al., 2020), and this holds true even for more diverse ecological communities under field conditions (Ushio, 2022a).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on the relationship between diversity and interaction strength.

claim: Coley and Aide, 1991 proposed that interactions between plants and insect herbivores were generally stronger in warmer regions.
source: In terrestrial ecosystems, Coley and Aide, 1991 proposed that interactions between plants and insect herbivores were generally stronger in warmer regions, which may result in stronger negative density dependence for tree species and contribute to higher plant diversity in a tropical region (Forrister et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites Coley and Aide's proposal about temperature effects on plant-herbivore interactions.

claim: Wieczynski et al., 2021 showed that species-level functional traits (e.g., body size and shape) may underlie the relationships between temperature and interaction strengths.
source: In addition, Wieczynski et al., 2021 showed that species-level functional traits (e.g., body size and shape) may underlie the relationships between temperature and interaction strengths.
evidence: The manuscript cites research linking functional traits to temperature-interaction strength relationships.

claim: Previous studies demonstrated that the quantity of eDNA may be a proxy of fish abundance and/or biomass.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that the quantity of eDNA may be a proxy of fish abundance and/or biomass (i.e., a positive correlation between the quantity of eDNA and fish abundance/biomass) (Takahara et al., 2012; Thomsen et al., 2012; Yamamoto et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research establishing eDNA as a proxy for fish abundance/biomass.

claim: Recent studies demonstrated that eDNA metabarcoding combined with frequent water sampling enabled the efficient monitoring of high-diversity ecological communities.
source: Recent studies demonstrated that eDNA metabarcoding combined with frequent water sampling enabled the efficient monitoring of high-diversity ecological communities (Bista et al., 2017; Djurhuus et al., 2020; Ushio, 2022a).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent studies on the effectiveness of eDNA metabarcoding for biodiversity monitoring.

claim: Recent studies have shown that information on interspecific interactions may be embedded in multispecies eDNA time series, particularly when the data are 'quantitative'.
source: More importantly, recent studies have shown that information on interspecific interactions may be embedded in multispecies eDNA time series, particularly when the data are 'quantitative' (Ushio, 2022a).
evidence: The manuscript cites research showing that quantitative eDNA time series contain interaction information.

claim: Transfer entropy (TE) is a method based on the information theory that quantifies information flow between two variables.
source: For example, transfer entropy (TE) is a method based on the information theory that quantifies information flow between two variables (Runge et al., 2012; Schreiber, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript describes transfer entropy as a method and cites foundational papers.

claim: Convergent cross mapping (CCM) is a causality detection tool in empirical dynamic modeling.
source: Convergent cross mapping (CCM) is a causality detection tool in empirical dynamic modeling (Sugihara et al., 2012), which is based on the dynamical theory.
evidence: The manuscript describes CCM as a causality detection method and cites the foundational paper.

claim: The multiview distance regularized (MDR) S-map enables accurate quantifications of interaction strengths of a large interaction network even when the number of network nodes exceeds the time series length.
source: In addition, an improved version of a sequentially weighted global linear map (S-map), called the multiview distance regularized (MDR) S-map, enables accurate quantifications of interaction strengths of a large interaction network even when the number of network nodes exceeds the time series length (Chang et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript describes the capabilities of the MDR S-map method and cites the relevant paper.

claim: The study hypothesized that a positive relationship exists between temperature and interaction strengths at the community level.
source: We hypothesized that (1) a positive relationship exists between temperature and interaction strengths at the community level, as found in other ecosystems and many types of interactions, and (2) the relationship between the patterns of temperature and interaction strengths varies among fish species because of species-specific ecologies and the behavior of component species.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the first hypothesis of the study.

claim: The study hypothesized that the relationship between the patterns of temperature and interaction strengths varies among fish species because of species-specific ecologies and behavior.
source: We hypothesized that (1) a positive relationship exists between temperature and interaction strengths at the community level, as found in other ecosystems and many types of interactions, and (2) the relationship between the patterns of temperature and interaction strengths varies among fish species because of species-specific ecologies and the behavior of component species.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the second hypothesis of the study.

claim: The interactions detected by the eDNA time series analysis at twice-monthly sampling frequency should have the same time scale and tend to focus on behavior-level interactions rather than birth–death processes.
source: As our eDNA time series was taken twice a month, the interactions detected should also have the same time scale (e.g., the interactions detected may cause changes in the population size at the same time scale), which means that we tend to focus on behavior-level interactions (e.g., feeding, vigilance, and schooling) rather than birth–death process in the present study (except for predation).
evidence: The manuscript explains the temporal scale of detected interactions based on sampling frequency.

claim: The interactions detected by the time series analysis could include various types of interactions such as competition and mutualism that could be involved in the population dynamics.
source: In addition, the interactions we detected by the time series analysis could include various types of interactions such as competition and mutualism that could be involved in the population dynamics.
evidence: The manuscript states that multiple types of interactions could be detected by the analysis.

claim: Seasonal changes in eDNA concentrations were consistent with the patterns of seasonal occurrences in tropical and subtropical fish species in the Boso Peninsula, which are transported by the warm Kuroshio Current, settling on the coastal waters during warmer months and subsequently disappearing during colder months.
source: Seasonal changes in eDNA concentrations were consistent with the patterns of seasonal occurrences in tropical and subtropical fish species in the Boso Peninsula, to which they are transported by the warm Kuroshio Current, settling on the coastal waters during the warmer months and subsequently disappearing during the colder months (Saito, 2019; Senou et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript explains seasonal eDNA patterns in the context of fish migration patterns, citing relevant literature.

claim: Water temperature may influence fish physiological activity.
source: Indeed, water temperature may influence fish physiological activity (Claireaux et al., 2006; Kishi et al., 2005; Oyugi et al., 2012) often in a complex way, and thus, the community-level influence of water temperature may also be complex as they should arise from the individual-level influence of water temperature on fish.
evidence: The manuscript states that temperature influences fish physiology, citing relevant literature.

claim: The direction (positive or negative) of the temperature effects on fish metabolic activities may be species specific.
source: In addition, the direction (i.e., positive or negative) of the temperature effects on fish metabolic activities may be species specific (Oyugi et al., 2012), and this species specificity may underlie the species-specific effects of temperature on the interaction strength.
evidence: The manuscript cites research showing species-specific temperature effects on fish metabolism.

claim: Water temperature has significant influences on marine community composition and diversity at the global spatial scale and historical time scale.
source: Water temperature has significant influences on marine community composition and diversity at the global spatial scale and historical time scale (Tittensor et al., 2010; Yasuhara and Deutsch, 2023), but the mechanism of temperature effects on fish community assembly is not fully understood.
evidence: The manuscript cites research on temperature effects on marine communities at large scales.

claim: Recent studies have shown that temperature (and oxygen) plays an important role in determining fish body size at the historical time scale.
source: Recent studies have shown that temperature (and oxygen) plays an important role in determining fish body size at the historical time scale (Salvatteci et al., 2022; Yasuhara and Deutsch, 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent research on temperature effects on fish body size.

claim: Fish body size plays a critical role in interspecific interactions such as predator–prey interactions.
source: As fish body size plays a critical role in interspecific interactions such as predator–prey interactions (e.g., predator–prey mass ratio; Nakazawa et al., 2011), temperature-induced body size changes may influence interspecific interactions at a longer time scale.
evidence: The manuscript states the importance of body size in interactions, citing relevant literature.

claim: The study showed that temperature may induce changes in fish–fish interactions at a relatively short time scale (weeks to months), perhaps via temperature effects on the physiological activity of fish individuals.
source: On the other hand, our study showed that temperature may induce changes in fish–fish interactions at a relatively short time scale (weeks to months), perhaps via temperature effects on the physiological activity of fish individuals.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about short-term temperature effects on interactions.

claim: Temperature effects on fish community assembly involve effects at different time scales.
source: These suggest that temperature effects on fish community assembly involve effects at different time scales, and thus, integrating results from different temporal (and spatial) scales are necessary to understand fish community assembly processes in nature.
evidence: The manuscript concludes that temperature effects operate at multiple time scales.

claim: The study revealed that temperature effects on fish–fish interactions depend on fish species identity.
source: In addition, our study revealed that temperature effects on fish–fish interactions depend on fish species identity.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes a key finding about species-specific temperature effects.

claim: Increased water temperature strengthens interactions received by Halichoeres tenuispinis and Microcanthus strigatus.
source: For example, increased water temperature strengthens interactions received by H. tenuispinis and M. strigatus (Figure 4), which may destabilize the population dynamics of these species.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific examples of species whose interactions strengthen with temperature, referencing Figure 4.

claim: Increased water temperature may destabilize the population dynamics of Halichoeres tenuispinis and Microcanthus strigatus.
source: For example, increased water temperature strengthens interactions received by H. tenuispinis and M. strigatus (Figure 4), which may destabilize the population dynamics of these species.

claim: The study provides a practical framework to quantify response diversity using time series.
source: Our study provides a practical framework to quantify response diversity using time series (the S-map method calculates the first derivative as an interaction strength, and it is an analog of the additive model-based method proposed by Ross et al., 2023), and quantifying species-specific responses to environmental changes and their diversity would be key to predicting the community-level responses under climate change.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodological contribution of the study for quantifying response diversity.

claim: The study demonstrated that the strengths of fish species interactions changed with water temperature under field conditions.
source: The present study demonstrated that the strengths of fish species interactions changed with water temperature under field conditions.

source: For several fish species, species interactions were intensified in warmer water and for some other fish species, species interactions were weakened in warmer water.

claim: For some fish species, species interactions were weakened in warmer water.

source: This may change the correlation and distribution of interaction strengths in a community, which may consequently influence community dynamics and stability in a complex way (Allesina et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2014; Ushio et al., 2018a).

claim: eDNA analysis is potentially applicable to any type of organisms even if they are difficult to be detected using traditional methods.
source: Developments and improvements in eDNA techniques and statistical analyses are still required; however, because eDNA analysis is potentially applicable to any type of organisms even if they are difficult to be detected using traditional methods, our framework integrating an eDNA analysis and advanced statistical analyses pave a way to understand and forecast dynamics of various ecological communities under field conditions.

claim: The framework integrating eDNA analysis and advanced statistical analyses paves a way to understand and forecast dynamics of various ecological communities under field conditions.

claim: Species-specific differences in the copy numbers of the genetic marker and eDNA release rates do not cause serious biases in the reconstruction of networks and estimations of interaction strengths because time series are standardized before analysis.
source: Our nonlinear time series analysis used the information embedded in fluctuations in time series, and time series are always standardized before the analysis. Therefore, species-specific differences in the copy numbers of the genetic marker and eDNA release rates, which may bias the estimation of absolute abundance, do not cause serious biases in the reconstruction of the networks and estimations of interaction strengths.
evidence: The manuscript explains why species-specific biases do not affect the analysis due to standardization.
